added_claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
added_claims.quote: most traditional portfolios assume linearity. They're looking for the straightest possible um equity curve, the most linear equity curve, the curve with the highest Sharpe ratio
added_claims.claim: Traditional portfolio construction assumes a linear input-output world and so targets the straightest equity curve with the highest Sharpe ratio, which is inconsistent with non-linear markets where payoff shape matters more than smoothness.
added_claims.testable: partly - compare Sharpe-optimised vs skew-optimised portfolios

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: there's too much bleed. It's too expensive to provide convexity on a daily basis because it doesn't matter uh in the long run
added_claims.claim: Counter-view on convexity horizon: longer-term managers can argue that supplying convexity at short horizons (daily) costs too much bleed and does not matter for long-run results, so convexity should be defined by time frame (Quantica has a paper on this).
added_claims.testable: yes - compare cost of short-horizon convexity with long-run payoff

added_claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
added_claims.quote: options is probably the purest way to get um protection for a traditional portfolio for adverse risk events because you can align the option exposure to what you're trying to protect
added_claims.claim: Options are the most precise hedge for a traditional portfolio because they can be matched to the specific risk (correlation risk, market risk), whereas trend following is a less targeted, free-of-premium form of convexity.
added_claims.testable: partly - hedge effectiveness vs cost testable

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: I mean, how many strategies in our careers have we really seen blow up completely?
added_claims.claim: Niels, citing Asness, pushes back that complete permanent loss of capital is rare in any strategy, so defining risk only that way is too narrow; he wants something in between because volatility can still feel like risk even if it is not the same.

added_claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
added_claims.quote: you could apply a process that applies it based on closed equity. Um the unrealized equity is not a problem with the new incoming investor.
added_claims.claim: Rich's answer to the new-investor problem: allocate new AUM using closed equity, so open (unrealised) equity stays with existing investors and is not a new investor's problem; there are different models for this.
added_claims.indicator: closed equity vs open equity for AUM allocation
added_claims.conditions: funds with large open trade equity from a few trades
added_claims.testable: partly - simulate new-investor drawdown under both bases

added_claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
added_claims.quote: do not do trend following unless you're prepared to do it for the long haul
added_claims.claim: The philosophy of trend following is long-horizon compounding with patience; using it for other purposes (as an allocation inside traditional portfolios, or managing outside AUM) adds concerns, which Rich calls the business of trend following as distinct from trend following itself.
added_claims.conditions: investors who cannot tolerate long drawdowns

added_claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
added_claims.quote: the principle there is a return that pays for all of the costs you've had over the course of time
added_claims.claim: Rich's aim is 'infinite yield': an open-ended payoff from letting profits run so that one trend pays for all accumulated costs of small controlled losses, which are the price of staying in the game for the next unknown opportunity.
added_claims.conditions: requires patience and survival through losing streaks
added_claims.testable: yes - profit factor of top trades vs cumulative losses

added_claims.speaker: Richard Brennan
added_claims.quote: is diversification as safety net. It's not only about a safety net, but it's also about spreading that net wide to capture those outliers, expanding the opportunity set, and also risk reduction through diversity.
added_claims.claim: Diversification in trend following serves three purposes: lower portfolio correlation and risk through diversity, a wider opportunity set, and capturing outliers wherever they appear.
added_claims.testable: yes - market count vs trend capture and risk

corrections.issue: Two speakers merged: Niels only raises the risk (new investors holding funds with 50-70% open trade equity face large drawdowns, and the principle suits one's own money with an infinite runway). The suggestion to allocate AUM on closed equity is Rich's reply, not Niels's.
corrections.fix: Niels: in funds whose open trade equity grew to 50-70% of NAV, new investors are exposed to a straight 50% drawdown that long-standing investors are not, so closed-equity sizing mainly suits own money; Rich replied separately that new AUM can be allocated on closed equity.

completeness_estimate: 0.88 - first reader captured nearly all of Rich's convexity argument and Niels' data and interjections; missed the Niels/Asness risk-definition pushback, Rich's reply on closed-equity AUM and long-haul philosophy, option-hedge precision, linearity assumption, infinite yield and diversification-as-safety-net, and merged two speakers in the open-equity claim.
